title: US and Israel Planning Bombing Campaign Against Iranian Energy Infrastructure
excerpt: Strikes on energy targets could begin as early as this weekend, CBS News reports, marking a significant escalation in the five-month-old conflict.
body:
• The US and Israel are planning a bombing campaign against energy infrastructure targets in Iran, with strikes possible throughout the weekend, according to CBS News.
  • The planned escalation comes after the collapse of a US-Iran interim ceasefire in June and renewed Iranian missile attacks on US forces this week.
  • The conflict has already disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea shipping routes, threatening global energy supplies and the Indian diaspora across the Gulf.
  • More than five months into the war, the Middle East energy sector appears weaker and more vulnerable than at any point since hostilities began.

A Weekend of Potential Strikes

The United States and Israel are preparing to launch a bombing campaign targeting energy-related infrastructure in Iran, with strikes possible throughout this weekend, CBS News reported on Friday, citing sources familiar with the planning.

The report represents a dramatic escalation in the five-month-old conflict that has already reshaped global energy markets and threatened the stability of one of the world's most strategically vital regions.

"The international community has entered a period of profound political and financial upheaval."

— UNAIDS, July 2026 report

Escalation After Failed Ceasefire

The planned strikes follow weeks of intensifying hostilities. An interim ceasefire deal between the US and Iran unraveled on June 17, and Washington renewed strikes against Iranian targets on Tuesday after Tehran and its allied militias attacked tankers and energy infrastructure, including two major refineries in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.

On Monday, the US military said it intercepted multiple ballistic missiles launched by Iran toward US forces in the Middle East. Iran's strike came soon after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met President Donald Trump at the White House, where Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz publicly stated that Israel had wanted to strike Iranian energy infrastructure but had been held back by the Trump administration.

A Conflict Reshaping Global Energy

The war, launched on February 28 when the US and Israel attacked Iran, has fundamentally altered the region's energy landscape. Iran responded with strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting US bases, and the conflict has since expanded from the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militia last week declared an embargo on Saudi oil exports in the Red Sea, potentially shutting a second major chokepoint for energy shipping. Attacks on tankers and energy assets have severely complicated shipments from Saudi Arabia's west coast, which had emerged as a critical alternative route after Hormuz was effectively shut earlier this year.

More than five months into the conflict, the region's energy sector appears weaker and more vulnerable than at any point since the war began. Importers are beginning to avoid supplies from a region that accounted for a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas exports before hostilities commenced.

Implications for the Indian Diaspora

The escalation carries direct consequences for the roughly nine million Indians living and working across the Gulf states. Previous rounds of strikes have triggered evacuations, disrupted flights, and raised concerns about the safety of Indian workers in the region.

India, which sources a significant portion of its crude oil from the Middle East, faces further pressure on its energy import bill as conflict-driven supply disruptions push global prices higher. The Indian government has been in contact with Gulf nations to ensure the safety of its nationals.

Trump, politically vulnerable to rising fuel prices ahead of November's midterm elections, paused strikes last weekend but threatened to restart unless negotiations delivered results. Iran has denied seeking to resume talks with Washington, and the latest reports suggest that pause has ended.
nri_angle: Indian Americans with family in the Gulf face growing disruption as the US-Iran conflict threatens regional energy markets and the safety of the large Indian expatriate community in the Middle East.
